https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/motherboard_marked.1424fb70adcd5cc9b3e3d12763f72fac6e9465a8a1acc1a096a99c9d268227a6_hu_a8d9651a569fef69.webp 1315w"><img class="title-image" alt="Motherboard" width="1315" height="700" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/motherboard_marked.1424fb70adcd5cc9b3e3d12763f72fac6e9465a8a1acc1a096a99c9d268227a6.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Motherboard with important parts labelled</figcaption></figure></div></figure><h3 class="tab-title">Diagram</h3><figure class="tab cover nested-single" id="cover-diagram"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/main.0a7c1c1f532346336f60abf62dc1366d4eb500aa88580fbec0229a25d78e2bf7.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/main.0a7c1c1f532346336f60abf62dc1366d4eb500aa88580fbec0229a25d78e2bf7_hu_68d582de1a7923e7.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/main.0a7c1c1f532346336f60abf62dc1366d4eb500aa88580fbec0229a25d78e2bf7_hu_b8b5d423ef5f630.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/main.0a7c1c1f532346336f60abf62dc1366d4eb500aa88580fbec0229a25d78e2bf7_hu_faa1fadf8f4a51c2.webp 1963w"><img class="title-image" alt="Diagram" width="1963" height="981" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/main.0a7c1c1f532346336f60abf62dc1366d4eb500aa88580fbec0229a25d78e2bf7.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption>Main architecture diagram<br>After the 'Slim' model, NAND and SDRAM size were doubled (to 64 MB each)</figcaption></figure></div></section><hr><h2 id="a-quick-introduction">A quick introduction</h2><p>Released just one month after the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-ds/">Nintendo DS</a>, Sony’s PSP proved that ‘horizontal innovation’ is not the only way to succeed in the portable console market.</p><p>This article is dedicated to anyone who wants to understand, straight to the point, how the PSP operates. It’s not a short write-up, but I hope that at the end of the article, you will be able to grasp the building blocks of this console (its design rationale, choice of CPUs, GPU pipeline, security system and so forth).</p><hr><h2 id="main-cpu">Main CPU</h2><p>Similarly to Nintendo, Sony built an <em>extremely packed</em> System-on-Chip (SoC) that houses most of the components we are going to discuss throughout this article. This includes the <strong>main CPU</strong> in charge of executing games and other programs (unlike the other CPUs, which we’ll talk about in due time). The SoC is called <strong>Tachyon</strong>, a name chosen by Sony themselves (after watching some <em>Star Trek</em>?).</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/tachyon.a7c25cb952548e37638dbaf3bf0dc7719c4e7824426d34c915caa5c5115a2677.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/tachyon.a7c25cb952548e37638dbaf3bf0dc7719c4e7824426d34c915caa5c5115a2677_hu_ae6c291b7f09213a.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/tachyon.a7c25cb952548e37638dbaf3bf0dc7719c4e7824426d34c915caa5c5115a2677_hu_c5f13c953de47168.webp 700w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="700" height="594" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/tachyon.a7c25cb952548e37638dbaf3bf0dc7719c4e7824426d34c915caa5c5115a2677.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The Tachyon chip on the original PSP model.</figcaption></figure><p>The main CPU is also an in-house design by Sony that <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#cpu">keeps up with the tradition</a> of using <strong>MIPS</strong> technology. Be as it may, it’s been four years since the release of the PlayStation 2, I wonder what’s the state of MIPS since then?</p><h3 id="mips-after-the-turn-of-the-century">MIPS after the turn of the century</h3><p>I’m afraid the golden years of MIPS have been kept in the 90s and there aren’t any indicators that these will repeat anytime soon. Its parent company, SGI, lost dominance against affordable x86 workstations and was running out of cash. So, in 1999 it sold its majority stake in MIPS <sup id="bibref:1"><a href="#bib:cpu-foremski" role="doc-biblioref">[1]</a></sup>. With this, MIPS became an independent company once again, however, the competition was more fierce than it was in the early days.</p><p>The company’s first decision was to acknowledge that MIPS CPUs couldn’t compute in the high-performance arena anymore. So, they shifted their focus to <strong>low-power computing</strong>, running head-to-head against <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#the-cambridge-miracle">ARM</a> and its <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-ds/#arms-new-territories">unprecedented popularity</a>.</p><p>Consequently, MIPS revisited its fragmented CPU line and consolidated it with <strong>three instruction sets</strong> <sup id="bibref:2"><a href="#bib:cpu-modern_mips" role="doc-biblioref">[2]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li><strong>MIPS32</strong>: An update of <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#the-offering">MIPS II</a> (the last 32-bit-only ISA) bringing functionality gathered from later architectures while keeping the 32-bit boundary.</li><li><strong>MIPS64</strong>: The continuation of MIPS V, a <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#cpu">64-bit ISA</a> and the last one before the revamp. The MIPS V has been a superset of all previous ISAs, just like its predecessors.</li><li><strong>microMIPS</strong>: Available as ‘microMIPS32’ and ‘microMIPS64’, these are supersets of the MIPS32 and MIPS64, respectively, with an additional group of 16-bit instructions (à la <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#tab-2-3-squeezing-performance">Thumb</a>). microMIPS is not binary compatible with the other ISAs, however. Thus, it would require re-compilation of legacy codebases to run on microMIPS.</li></ul><p>The big difference was that these would now be developed in conjunction, as opposed to MIPS dropping the previous architecture as soon as the next one arrived. New revisions would be denoted with the ‘Release x’ suffix, such as ‘MIPS32 Release 6’ or ‘MIPS32R6’ (coincidentally, the last revision to date).</p><p>Along with the ISAs, MIPS also started selling a new line of IP cores. For instance, the <strong>MIPS32 4k</strong> design implemented the <strong>MIPS32 R2 ISA</strong>, it came in different variants and offered plenty of customisations.</p><p>Back on topic, Sony presumably acquired a license of the MIPS32 4k and customised it by extending the ISA and bundling particular co-processors <sup id="bibref:3"><a href="#bib:cpu-gcc_patch" role="doc-biblioref">[3]</a></sup>. The result is called <strong>Allegrex</strong> and runs at a variable speed, from <strong>33 MHz to 333 MHz</strong>.</p><h3 id="the-new-portable-cpu">The new portable CPU</h3><p>Allegrex is a complete 32-bit core offering <sup id="bibref:4"><a href="#bib:cpu-hitmen" role="doc-biblioref">[4]</a></sup> <sup id="bibref:5"><a href="#bib:cpu-naked" role="doc-biblioref">[5]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li>A <strong>custom MIPS ISA</strong>: mixes MIPS32R2 instructions with exclusive ones for <strong>arithmetic operations</strong> (multiplication, subtraction, min/max, bit-shifts) and <strong>interrupt control</strong>. These are called ‘Allegrex Extended Instructions’.</li><li>A <strong>32-bit address bus</strong>: this means that up to 4 GB of memory can be seen by this CPU.</li><li><strong>32 general-purpose registers</strong>: all of them store 32-bit numbers; and two (the zero register and link register) are reserved for special uses. By now, this should come as no surprise.</li><li>A <strong>7-stage pipeline</strong> (one more than its <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#a-special-order-for-sony">home sibling</a>). <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#tab-2-1-the-core">Here</a> is a previous explanation of CPU pipelining if you’d like to know more.</li><li><strong>32 KB of L1 Cache</strong>: of which 16 KB is for instructions and 16 KB for data.</li><li>A <strong>cache write-back buffer</strong>: the CPU can write over cache believing it has updated physical memory as well. Then, the cache takes care of updating memory when the buffer is full.<ul><li>This design speeds up memory stores, but doesn’t work right away with multi-processor systems like the PSP. So, developers will have to take care of evicting the buffer when other components require those new values in memory.</li></ul></li></ul><p>This looks way more competitive than the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-ds/#cpu">ARM9-based alternative</a>, but it’s not over yet, as we still need to check the co-processors <em>cooperating</em> next to the core.</p><h3 id="coprocessors">Coprocessors</h3><p>As with any MIPS CPU, Allegrex has three coprocessor slots. Sony added three:</p><ul><li>The <strong>System Control Coprocessor</strong> as ‘CP0’: a <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#tab-2-1-system-control-coprocessor">necessary building block</a> of any MIPS CPU. This particular component is what enables memory protection, cache coherency and interrupt control in the core itself <sup id="bibref:6"><a href="#bib:cpu-mips_4k" role="doc-biblioref">[6]</a></sup>.</li><li>A <strong>Floating Point Unit</strong> (FPU) as ‘CP1’: accelerates arithmetic operations with 32-bit decimal numbers (following the IEEE 754 standard). It has <strong>thirty-two 32-bit registers</strong> and an <strong>independent 8-stage pipeline</strong>, thereby adding more parallelism to the main CPU.</li><li>A <strong>Vector Floating Point Unit</strong> (VFPU) as ‘CP2’: a coprocessor designed for <strong>vector operations</strong>, similar to a traditional SIMD processor. Compared to the FPU, it instead provides <strong>128 32-bit registers</strong>, relies on a proprietary instruction set and implements a variable-length pipeline. The VFPU operates up to 32-bit floating-point values, which can be grouped into a 4-component vector or <strong>even a 4x4 matrix</strong> (useful for different kinds of geometric operations without requiring to re-arrange the data).<ul><li>Its efficiency comes from its 128-bit data bus connected to the rest of the system, offloading the main CPU’s transit.</li><li>Unlike the FPU, some behaviour of the VFPU deviates from the IEEE-754 standard.</li></ul></li></ul><p>In conclusion: Allegrex is incredibly fast. However, we still don’t know what can you do with it. After all, you can imagine this CPU as the conductor of an orchestra, and we haven’t checked out the performers yet.</p><h4 id="focused-memory-management">Focused memory management</h4><p>Let me talk for a moment about the memory system implemented in this system. Among other things, the System Control Coprocessor provides the functionality of a <strong>Memory Protection Unit</strong> or ‘MPU’ (not to be confused with an ‘MMU’), this maps the physical hardware onto the CPU’s memory space with some special quirks in between. Even though its <em>modus operandi</em> can be seen as a bit primitive at first, we’ll see why it’s optimal for the needs of this console.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/cpu/mmu.e203e0ea6a6aa12161940cb314ea9c88176dedc87bc67686ae73513c953a756e.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="760" height="215" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/cpu/mmu.e203e0ea6a6aa12161940cb314ea9c88176dedc87bc67686ae73513c953a756e.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Memory addressing with the MPU.</figcaption></figure><p>A traditional Memory Management Unit or ‘MMU’ takes care of the CPU’s access to the components surrounding it. This implies that all the address lines of the CPU will be connected to the MMU; only the latter is connected to the rest of the system.</p><p>This is particularly advantageous for features like ‘virtual memory’ and ‘memory protection’. Well, to achieve virtual memory, an MMU must contain a component called ‘Translation Look-aside Buffer’ (TLB) to prevent performance degradation. Now, <strong>Allegrex’s MMU lacks a TLB</strong>, so it focuses on memory protection. This is why Allegrex’s MMU is instead called an MPU (Memory Protection Unit). An MPU is a cut-down version of an MMU without virtual memory. In any case, <strong>memory protection gives the system the power to decide which memory locations a program can access</strong>.</p><p>Thanks to this, Allegrex won’t have to deal with userland programs (i.e. games) accessing restricted locations (i.e. encryption keys). To accomplish the restriction itself, memory addresses are grouped into five segments with different privilege levels. Furthermore, Allegrex’s MPU contains three modes of operation: <strong>User mode</strong>, <strong>Supervisor mode</strong> and <strong>Kernel mode</strong>.</p><p>If a normal process (operating in user mode) wants to access a memory address found in a privileged location, the MPU will ask the operating system (through the use of ‘exceptions’) whether to grant permission to the process.</p><p>All in all, this allows Sony, the developer of the operating system, to implement a security system enforced by hardware.</p><h3 id="memory-available">Memory available</h3><p>So far we’ve analysed the PSP’s main CPU and its accelerators. Now let’s see the physical memory available in this system.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/cpu/memory.fbca10a233424ccc4abe3d5a6d86f7613c9b86af7c53dde37ecdd5511ea0eae2.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="577" height="248" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/cpu/memory.fbca10a233424ccc4abe3d5a6d86f7613c9b86af7c53dde37ecdd5511ea0eae2.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Memory layout from the main CPU perspective.</figcaption></figure><p>The PSP comes with two memory blocks accessible from the CPU:</p><ul><li><strong>16 KB of SRAM</strong>: this is what we called <strong>Scratchpad</strong> in <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#cpu">previous articles</a>. It’s small but very fast RAM. It’s up to developers to make proper use of it, although unofficial documents called it ‘useless’.</li><li><strong>32 MB of DDR SDRAM</strong>: it’s huge and many other components will make use of it, but since it’s not that close to the CPU, its access rate is slower. We’ll refer to it as ‘main memory’ across the article.<ul><li>The ‘DDR’ initials mean ‘Double Data Rate’, which denotes an evolution from the traditional ‘SDRAM’, featuring a faster transfer protocol. The <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox/#memory-layout">original Xbox</a> used the same type.</li></ul></li></ul><h3 id="bus-design">Bus design</h3><p>You’ll soon find that the PSP accommodates lots of components with unique functionality. So, to organise them without repeating <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#tab-3-1-pipeline-stalls">previous mistakes</a>, engineers interconnected them using dedicated buses. Thus, only small groups of components, with similar applications, will share the same bus. Those buses talk to each other using dedicated arbiters (in the form of ‘memory controllers’ or Direct Memory Access (DMA)).</p><p>All of the buses found in Tachyon implement a well-known design called <strong>Advanced High-performance Bus</strong> (AHB), a solution built by Arm to tackle congestion on their chips and SoCs. If you are curious, AHBs are also used in the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#io">Wii</a>.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/cpu/buses.789eeb69ea63519a446c61d5178b75f1cd9af2162f635cfc537e0eba1caf7534.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="736" height="167" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/cpu/buses.789eeb69ea63519a446c61d5178b75f1cd9af2162f635cfc537e0eba1caf7534.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Basic layout of the three main buses in this system.</figcaption></figure><p>Using the principles above, the following buses were constructed for the PSP:</p><ul><li>The <strong>System Bus</strong>: connects the CPU, scratchpad and GPU. It’s 128 bits wide.</li><li>The <strong>Media Engine bus</strong>: connects another group of components (explained in the next section). It has the same properties as the System Bus.</li><li>The <strong>Peripheral Bus</strong>: connects I/O and storage-related components. It’s 32-bits wide.</li></ul><p>All three buses connect to the DDR controller, which is where the main RAM is found.</p><h3 id="tackling-traffic-congestion">Tackling traffic congestion</h3><p>Inside each bus, there will be multiple components working independently. They will store processed data in a shared space (such as the main RAM). Now, we don’t want the CPU to intervene whenever a module needs to read or write from memory. Traditionally, a DMA unit was placed in the bus to provide this facility, but a single DMA can only do so much. The PSP contains a significant number of components, and this will eventually lead to bottlenecks.</p><p>The solution is very simple: <strong>bus mastering</strong>. In a nutshell, each component will get its own DMA controller. This gives them the ability to become the ‘bus master’ and take control of the bus to access whatever location they want. To avoid contention (multiple ‘bus masters’ at the same time), the neighbouring components will acknowledge this event and wait until the operation completes.</p><h3 id="the-end-of-the-line">The end of the line</h3><p>The RISC revolution spawned countless CPUs throughout the 80s-90s but only a handful lasted after the turn of the century. Just like I <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/dreamcast/#end-of-the-line">concluded my analysis of the SuperH</a> in the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/dreamcast/">Dreamcast article</a>, <strong>the PlayStation Portable will be my last article of this series carrying a MIPS CPU</strong>.</p><p>After many turnarounds, what’s left of MIPS is now a company designing <strong>RISC-V</strong> CPUs. In all fairness, this is an interesting strategy that provides the company with greater leverage to compete against ARM.</p><p>Looking back at my analyses, however, it’s hard to comprehend how such a talented company could’ve lost its market share. Admittedly, in the workstation market, it became clear that Intel’s x86, no matter the amount of criticism, won by making equipment affordable (thanks to its Pentium line, along with the ‘clones’) and attractive due to its (Windows-only) compatible software. Finally, the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox/#tab-1-4-cisc-or-risc">P6 architecture</a> provided Intel with the scalability initially only enjoyed by RISC designs.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/mips_interview.93f63f50948294794d1dba0572cc6d782ca86f2b4b07a1ae684f775076d04501.jpeg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/mips_interview.93f63f50948294794d1dba0572cc6d782ca86f2b4b07a1ae684f775076d04501_hu_2d4b947d9ec26d0f.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/mips_interview.93f63f50948294794d1dba0572cc6d782ca86f2b4b07a1ae684f775076d04501_hu_4657596c84a0e524.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/mips_interview.93f63f50948294794d1dba0572cc6d782ca86f2b4b07a1ae684f775076d04501_hu_3d5dd22157711c3c.webp 1280w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1280" height="720" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/mips_interview.93f63f50948294794d1dba0572cc6d782ca86f2b4b07a1ae684f775076d04501.jpeg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">In 2011, the Computer History Museum (Mountain View, California) conducted an interesting interview with MIPS co-founders and former executives <sup id="bibref:7"><a href="#bib:cpu-chm_mips" role="doc-biblioref">[7]</a></sup>, where they talked about MIPS’ beginnings, its impact on the industry and eventual reorganisation.</figcaption></figure><p>In the case of low-power computing, it was more difficult for me to understand the retreat, as MIPS and ARM shared similar business models (IP licensing). Luckily, a previous interview from the Computer History Museum in 2011 also brought up the same question, resulting in this answer:</p><blockquote><p>We made a mistake, we didn’t realise how important the cellphone market was. Early there was no money to be made (…) but ARM got it by <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#tab-1-2-a-new-cpu-venture">investing in it</a>. It was a very smart move and it turned out to be incredible leverage point. We just looked at the gross margin and said “that’s not a great return! we’d be better off putting our attention elsewhere” but of course, it turned out cell phones became smartphones [and then] became a gigantic. <sup id="bibref:8"><a href="#bib:cpu-chm_mips" role="doc-biblioref">[8]</a></sup></p><p>– <cite>John Hennessy, co-founder of MIPS Computer Systems</cite></p></blockquote><p>Nevertheless, when it comes to this topic, I believe that, while we won’t see a new MIPS CPU, we’ll see the result of its former engineers transmitting its distinctive technology into new projects.</p><p>That being said, let’s take a look at the rest of the PSP components.</p><hr><h2 id="multimedia-cpu">Multimedia CPU</h2><p>Up to this point, we’ve discussed the main CPU and the buses inside Tachyon, but there are still many features to be found in the SoC. In particular, there’s another block of modules designed for a specific application: <strong>multimedia</strong>. This group specialises in <strong>audio and image processing</strong>, including the combination of both (video processing), and it operates without consuming bandwidth from the main CPU group (the ‘system group’).</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/games/daxter.1cc7d9cf70d1b049affab4a0affcfbfebe71bbf9bb35f7e20a2adaf17b691d7e.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="480" height="272" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/games/daxter.1cc7d9cf70d1b049affab4a0affcfbfebe71bbf9bb35f7e20a2adaf17b691d7e.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Daxter (2006).<br>In-game cinematic rendered with this block.</figcaption></figure><p>That being said, the new block is called <strong>Media Engine group</strong> and it’s composed of the following components:</p><ul><li>A second <strong>Allegrex CPU</strong> serving as the ‘controller’ of the Media Engine group. This is the same CPU found in the system group, but without the vector coprocessor <sup id="bibref:9"><a href="#bib:cpu-marshall" role="doc-biblioref">[9]</a></sup>. The controller is responsible for receiving orders from the main CPU and managing the rest of the multimedia hardware that will work concurrently.</li><li><strong>2 MB of eDRAM</strong>: multimedia encoding and/or decoding consumes a considerable amount of bandwidth, so to avoid stalling the other components, the Media Engine contains dedicated memory to process the data ‘in-house’ and publish the results once it’s necessary to do so.<ul><li>‘eDRAM’ is the same as DRAM but manufactured inside another chip.</li></ul></li><li>An <strong>MPEG-AVC</strong> decoder: a hardware decoder that does only one thing, and fast. That is, swallow <strong>H.264 video stream</strong> <sup id="bibref:10"><a href="#bib:cpu-ppsspp" role="doc-biblioref">[10]</a></sup> and spit out data that the audio and graphics endpoint understand.</li><li>A <strong>Virtual Mobile Engine</strong> or ‘VME’: this is <em>some sort</em> of programmable Digital Signal Processor (DSP). The controller programs it and then starts feeding in the data. Afterwards, like the AVC, the VME stores the processed chunk in local memory.<ul><li>This is a very obscure component; only Sony seems to know the ins and outs of it (including how to program it). To this day, it’s still a mystery.</li><li>From what it seems to be Sony’s leaked slides <sup id="bibref:11"><a href="#bib:cpu-specs" role="doc-biblioref">[11]</a></sup>, the VME seems to have local memory and a DMA controller. It’s also known as the ‘Dynamic Reconfigurable Engine’.</li></ul></li></ul><p>Needless to say, the Media Engine is not directly operable from the developer’s side (Sony hides all of it through a thick API). The official Software Development Kit (SDK) includes libraries like ‘libmpeg’ or ‘libmp3’ which already implement complete applications optimised for this engine.</p><hr><h2 id="graphics">Graphics</h2><p>To begin with, let’s go over the physical screen of this console, which is where the user can appreciate everything that will be discussed in this section.</p><h3 id="display">Display</h3><p>The PSP carries a <strong>4.3” TFT LCD screen</strong>. It has a resolution of <strong>480x272 pixels</strong> (for reference, that’s ~2.6 times the pixels of one screen of the Nintendo DS) and can display up to 16,777,216 colours. Thus, it’s got a 24-bit colour depth (the so-called ‘true color’ scale).</p><p>The aspect ratio is <em>almost</em> 16:9, a format which during that time was increasingly becoming standard on home TVs. Notice that a wider range of view is also an opportunity for game designers to improve the experience (especially in the first-person shooting genre).</p><h3 id="introducing-the-graphics-engine">Introducing the Graphics Engine</h3><p>Now it’s time to talk about the component in charge of producing pixels, the <strong>Graphics Engine</strong> (GE). The engine is found within the ‘system group’, so you may see it as a ‘group within a group’. Below you can see some of the results it achieved:</p><figure class="tabs nested centered-container"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-1-1-kh-link" class="active"><a All rendered at their maximum resolution (480x272 pixels).</figcaption></figure><p>The GE draws 3D graphics (polygons) with many features applied (texture mapping, lighting and so much more), which you’ll see in a bit.</p><h3 id="architecture-of-the-graphics-engine">Architecture of the Graphics Engine</h3><p>The GE subsystem has lots of interesting quirks to mention, so this will be a very complex section. But fear not! I’ll try to go step-by-step to avoid any confusion.</p><p>First things first – the GE is made of three components:</p><ul><li>The <strong>graphics core</strong>: where the actual graphics functionality happens.</li><li>The <strong>eDRAM controller</strong>: mediates access between eDRAM memory and the core.</li><li>The <strong>bus matrix</strong>: works as a ‘bus arbiter’ between the System Bus and the internals of the GE (remember the GE is found within the system group).<ul><li>In reality, this component is a mesh of wires with some logic, but for the sake of explaining, it’s simpler to mask with a black box.</li></ul></li></ul><p>The reason for this design is that both main CPU and the graphics core can access those 2 MB of eDRAM. So, to prevent congestion, the traffic inside the GE goes through another Advanced High-performance Bus called <strong>local bus</strong> (‘local’ from the perspective of the GE). This allows the graphics core to perform its functions without depending on the System Bus to move data around (and consequently stalling the rest of the system).</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/ge_arch.d963ccf084e42ace788d5bee3d16e6ad4391891b473f9f05a0f442dcae0df645.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="718" height="561" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/ge_arch.d963ccf084e42ace788d5bee3d16e6ad4391891b473f9f05a0f442dcae0df645.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Architecture of the Graphics Engine.</figcaption></figure><p>The local bus is as wide as the System Bus (128 bits), but if that wasn’t enough, the graphics core has a direct line to eDRAM using a 512-bit bus (made of two unidirectional 256-bit buses). You’ll see why it will be needed in the following section.</p><p>What about how the CPU and GE communicate with each other? As I said before, both CPU and graphics core can read from eDRAM. Additionally, the graphics core can access the System Bus to fetch data from any other component (including the main RAM). So, all of that just doesn’t happen magically.</p></div><p>In a nutshell, two <strong>bus matrix</strong> blocks re-wire the connection between the local bus and the System Bus. Whenever there’s a component that wants to access an ‘alien’ bus, the bus matrices configure the communication so that one unit becomes master of the two buses and no other overlaps, this persists until the designated unit finishes transferring memory.</p><p>This behaviour reminds me of the commonly known technique called <strong>bus mastering</strong>, where the leading component is the ‘bus master’ and has complete control of the bus, and the rest are ‘slaves’ waiting for commands. However, I’m not sure which protocol/standard Sony’s engineers were trying to replicate. Based on my understanding, I think it may be somewhat similar to I²C, a protocol used for serial communications (particularly useful with embedded systems) that also performs bus mastering.</p><h3 id="organising-the-content">Organising the content</h3><p>Now that we’ve seen what components we’ve got and how they interact with each other, let’s find out what information related to graphics we can place in memory.</p><p>There are three memory locations from which the GE will end up pulling from or filling:</p><ul><li><strong>2 MB eDRAM</strong>: the aforementioned eDRAM. It’s used to store the frame-buffer, <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#modern-visible-surface-determination">z-buffer</a> and texture buffer. Its contents are directly written by the GE. This memory space is also called ‘local memory’.<ul><li>The CPU can access this memory if needed, although its speed is not ideal.</li></ul></li><li><strong>32 MB DDR SDRAM</strong>: this is the working area of the CPU for building display lists, vertex data, texture data and CLUTs (Colour lookup tables). In the context of graphics, this bloc is called ‘host memory’.</li><li><strong>16 KB SRAM</strong>: the scratchpad memory is also accessible by both CPU and GE.</li></ul><h3 id="functionality">Functionality</h3><p>Like its <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#graphics">home sibling</a>, the PSP’s graphics system focuses on <strong>rasterisation</strong>. However, the PSP’s VRAM is half the size of the PS2’s, and its bus is not as fast. To compensate, the PSP’s Graphics Engine features a vector processor!</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/pipeline.9225d35b3f8a57b90212d0ad3f3c02154c12d50b003e58613b1106f9d138eaa0.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="745" height="561" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/pipeline.9225d35b3f8a57b90212d0ad3f3c02154c12d50b003e58613b1106f9d138eaa0.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Pipeline design of the Graphics Engine.<br>I’ve skipped the interfaces since it’s becoming too convoluted.</figcaption></figure><p>The graphics pipeline is very similar to that of the PS2, with the addition of the vector processing stage. The graphics core is divided into two areas: the <strong>surface engine</strong>, which deals with vector processing, and the <strong>rendering engine</strong> which, as its name indicates, performs rasterisation and effects.</p><p>Although its features have been explained in the past <sup id="bibref:12"><a href="#bib:cpu-programming" role="doc-biblioref">[12]</a></sup>, the details of the graphics pipeline itself have not. The truth is, programmers don’t depend on that information to build their games. However, for the sake of this analysis, I’ve deduced a model myself.</p><p>On another note, I’ve decided to make it a bit more technical than previous articles. I thought this would be a good opportunity to learn new concepts and have a wider vision of computing graphics. Having said that, I strongly recommend reading about the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#graphics">PS1</a> and <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#graphics">PS2</a> graphics systems before continuing.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-1-1-commands-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-1-1-commands">Commands</a></li><li id="tab-1-2-vector-processing-link"><a href="#tab-1-2-vector-processing">Vector Processing</a></li><li id="tab-1-3-rasterisation-link"><a href="#tab-1-3-rasterisation">Rasterisation</a></li><li id="tab-1-4-textures-link"><a href="#tab-1-4-textures">Textures</a></li><li id="tab-1-5-pixel-operations-link"><a href="#tab-1-5-pixel-operations">Pixel Operations</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-1-1-commands"><h4 id="tab-1-1-commands" class="tab-title">Commands</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/commands.3acff49963e1afe64ccf3778448e685b2efd8a82276eb947ce90b1ac7204d787.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="542" height="338" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/commands.3acff49963e1afe64ccf3778448e685b2efd8a82276eb947ce90b1ac7204d787.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Command stage.</figcaption></figure><p>The Graphics Engine is controlled using traditional ‘display lists’ stored in main memory. The CPU builds them and the GPU reads them (using Direct Memory Access). Display lists basically tell the GPU what, how and where to draw. In the case of the PSP, display lists are not limited to rendering tasks – they can also include vector transformations.</p><p>The strategy implemented to process lists is critical to ensure that the CPU and GPU work concurrently and don’t stall each other. Remember, we want the GPU to accelerate operations, not to be a burden. Hence, the CPU and GPU support <strong>deferred rendering</strong>, a technique that allows the CPU to build the next set of display lists while the GPU is processing a previous one. The GE is configured by specifying where in memory the display list starts (base address) and where it stops (stall address). As a result, there are two ways of allocating a list:</p><ul><li><strong>Double buffered</strong>: there are two separate display lists areas. One is being transferred to the GPU, the other is being filled by the CPU. When both processors finish, they swap places.</li><li><strong>Store controlled</strong>: the CPU fills the same list the DMA unit is transferring to the CPU, but the CPU is some entries ahead to avoid overlapping. This uses less memory but it’s susceptible to stalls if the GPU catches up.</li></ul><p>Furthermore, Sony stated that the GPU’s DMA unit is not just a ‘dumb memory copier’ – it can also understand the data transferred <sup id="bibref:13"><a href="#bib:cpu-programming" role="doc-biblioref">[13]</a></sup>. Thus, display lists can include <strong>commands</strong> such as <code>jump</code> and <code>return</code> to tell the DMA to branch out and get data from somewhere else. This saves the CPU from embedding large resources (models, textures, etc.) in the display lists (which would effectively duplicate data in memory) and reduces bandwidth consumption. This system was inherited from the PS2.</p><p>Finally, the DMA can also interpret <strong>bounding box data</strong>: combined with information stored in the GE, the DMA will skip drawing commands that aren’t within the display area. It’s also possible to declare bounding boxes inside other bounding boxes, but let’s leave that topic for another day!</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-2-vector-processing">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-2-vector-processing"><h4 id="tab-1-2-vector-processing" class="tab-title">Vector Processing</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/vector.513aba36c930069c928522d3043d4e4507b24a90d6d99859c3a0f1cbdd58ba3d.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="468" height="481" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/vector.513aba36c930069c928522d3043d4e4507b24a90d6d99859c3a0f1cbdd58ba3d.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Vector Processing stage.</figcaption></figure><p>The Graphics Engine debuts the ability to perform operations over vectors, which helps to offload a lot of work from the CPU. Sony built this unit to accelerate common tasks previously carried out by the PS2’s VPUs using microcode <sup id="bibref:14"><a href="#bib:cpu-programming" role="doc-biblioref">[14]</a></sup>. While the GE is not as flexible as a VPU (the GE is a fixed-function unit), it does simplify a lot of coding (considering microcode had a considerable weight on the learning curve). The GE’s vector processor is called <strong>surface engine</strong>.</p><p>The surface engine undertakes <strong>three types of task</strong>. The first is the operation of <strong>parametric surfaces</strong> <sup id="bibref:15"><a href="#bib:graphics-pspdkgu" role="doc-biblioref">[15]</a></sup>. Remember the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#infinite-worlds">‘Infinite Worlds’</a> section? Well, Sony explained that, while the PS2 was indeed capable of this, in the end just a few games bothered. It’s possible that polygon performance, along with difficulty in design and implementation, were the main factors.</p><p>To tackle this, the surface engine implements two parametric curves:</p><ul><li><strong>Bézier</strong>: a relatively fast function but its parameters change the global shape. Additionally, it suffers from ‘continuity issues’ which manifest as cracks on surfaces (discouraging its use with animations). It’s often used for landscape generation.</li><li><strong>B-spline</strong>: requires more computations but fixes continuity issues and provides localised control. Character modelling and animation are potential candidates.</li></ul><p>Both support <strong>levels of detail</strong>, which means that developers can set an arbitrary value to alter the level of subdivision (impacting the quality of the resulting model).</p><p>The second task is called <strong>vertex blending</strong>, a technique used for <strong>animations</strong>. The surface engine provides two types:</p><ul><li><strong>Skinning</strong> (a.k.a skeleton animation): movement relies on a structure of ‘joints’ attached to the character model. It’s often applied for normal animation (walking, jumping, etc.).</li><li><strong>Morphing</strong>: uses multiple instances of a model and averages them to get a ‘transition effect’ (using linear interpolation). It’s normally used for artificial animation (i.e. facial movement) and special effects. It comes with larger memory consumption and a steeper learning curve.</li></ul><p>It’s important to denote that the CPU may still need to compute animations to process game logic (e.g. collision detection), so the CPU can’t offload all the work.</p><p>Finally, the surface engine provides <strong>scissoring</strong> (discarding vertices outside the viewport/rectangular area) as well.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-1-commands">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-3-rasterisation">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-3-rasterisation"><h4 id="tab-1-3-rasterisation" class="tab-title">Rasterisation</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/rendering.68908e4f59bd7d4c3d463ddc2d8f31ca2c1bb1a45da713d5004924dde15ddb69.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="468" height="431" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/rendering.68908e4f59bd7d4c3d463ddc2d8f31ca2c1bb1a45da713d5004924dde15ddb69.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Rasterising stage.</figcaption></figure><p>The next stage of graphics generation takes place in the <strong>rendering engine</strong> (skipping the command processor). In here, vector data is transformed into pixels, which is pretty much in pace with any other GPU in the market.</p><p>The engine draws many types of primitives, including points, lines, line strips, triangles, triangle strips, triangle fans and, finally, sprites (made of 2D rectangles). It also contains a unit called ‘digital differential analyser’ that will be used for interpolating values during rasterisation and texture mapping.</p><p>Developers can supply a projection matrix to apply <strong>perspective transformation</strong>. This sends their 3D world to a 2D space (so you can see it on the screen), using the virtual camera as a model.</p><p>Sony didn’t provide much information about how its rasteriser works in particular, so it’s not well-known how many pixels are processed per cycle, for instance. Modern features, like sub-pixel precision, are assumed to be implemented (otherwise, users would’ve been able to <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation/#tab-4-1-distorted-modelstextures">spot its absence</a> right away).</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-2-vector-processing">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-4-textures">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-4-textures"><h4 id="tab-1-4-textures" class="tab-title">Textures</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/textures.3059f03139a77530cd12b9a8d7f8704a0c7c8e0dab127b57a920a4f9b471e93d.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="575" height="369" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/textures.3059f03139a77530cd12b9a8d7f8704a0c7c8e0dab127b57a920a4f9b471e93d.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Texture mapping stage.</figcaption></figure><p>This may be the topic of most interest for some. Polygons (now mere pixels) can be painted with textures. At this stage, texture maps are fetched from memory and processed with many functions. This process is called <strong>texture mapping</strong>.</p><p>The rendering engine has three <strong>mapping modes</strong> or, in other words, three ways of processing texture maps:</p><ul><li><strong>UV mapping</strong>: every coordinate of the model is mapped to a coordinate of the texture.</li><li><strong>Projective mapping</strong>: in a nutshell, it simulates a physical projector shining the texture map over a surface.</li><li><strong>Shade mapping</strong>: casts up to four lights (ambient, directional, point or spot) on the model. This is useful when blending the result with another map (you’ll see more in the next section).<ul><li>If programmers supply a texture map instead of a solid colour, you get a ‘fish eye’ effect (useful for reflections, a.k.a. <strong>environmental mapping</strong>).</li><li>This mode also permits <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#creativity">toon shading</a>.</li></ul></li></ul><p>Textures may use <strong>Colour Lookup Tables</strong> or ‘CLUTs’. Furthermore, this engine applies <strong>perspective correction</strong> and <strong>bilinear or trilinear filtering</strong> for interpolation.</p><p>On another topic, there’s <strong>8 KB of texture cache</strong> found in the GE to save bandwidth. It uses the ‘least recently used’ method for space management.</p><p>Finally, while this pipeline is not programmable, developers can send extra colours to be blended with textures. There’s also colour doubling (which doubles the RGB value of colours), colour addition (combines a primary colour with a secondary colour) and <strong>fogging</strong> (haze over distant polygons).</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-3-rasterisation">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-5-pixel-operations">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-5-pixel-operations"><h4 id="tab-1-5-pixel-operations" class="tab-title">Pixel Operations</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/operation.4d848a1cf7e348a24ab0f161f18486184e8de451b7be52e9f0c927946247ea2d.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="613" height="449" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/_diagrams/gpu/operation.4d848a1cf7e348a24ab0f161f18486184e8de451b7be52e9f0c927946247ea2d.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Pixel operation stage.</figcaption></figure><p>We’re reaching the end of the pipeline. The initial geometry has been transformed into pixels and these are now rich-coloured, so it’s time to decide what to do with them.</p><p>Some pixels may correspond to geometry that is not needed for this frame (it might be occluded, masked, etc.). To filter that out, the GE can perform the following tests:</p><ul><li><strong>Scissoring</strong>: discards polygons away from an arbitrary area.</li><li><strong>Depth range</strong>: discards too distant or too near polygons (developers set the reference values).</li><li><strong>Colour</strong>: discards pixels equal or not equal to an RGB value.</li><li><strong>Alpha</strong>: compares the pixel’s alpha value to a reference value.</li><li><strong>Stencil</strong>: similar to alpha, but relies on the stencil value.</li><li><strong>Depth test</strong>: late <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#modern-visible-surface-determination">Z-buffering</a>.</li></ul><p>Afterwards, pixels will also travel through these optional blocks for further effects:</p><ul><li><strong>Alpha blending</strong>: combines non-opaque pixels with the ones in the frame-buffer using different arithmetic operators.</li><li><strong>Dithering</strong>: softens colour changes.</li><li><strong>Colour clamping</strong>: aligns RGB values to fit in the frame-buffer format.</li><li><strong>Logical operation</strong>: decides how to merge the new frame with the existing frame-buffer using logical operators (<code>AND</code>, <code>OR</code> and many more).</li><li><strong>Masking</strong>: as the name indicates, it masks the z-buffer or frame-buffer.</li></ul><p>Complex functions like <strong>antialiasing</strong> are the result of a strategic combination of the above. Finally, the outputted pixel is written to the frame-buffer, which in turn is sent for display.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-4-textures">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h4 id="observations">Observations</h4><p>As evidenced, the PSP inherits various features from the PS2. The difference, however, is that functionality is now hardwired in the silicon, as opposed to offering many general-purpose programmable units (which require manual work to set them up). I presume this was done for two reasons: to use fewer transistors (so it fits in Tachyon and the board remains ‘portable’) and to facilitate porting PS2 codebases to the new console.</p><h3 id="interactive-models">Interactive models</h3><p>To show how this system impacted model design and to help compare it to the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#better-models">PS2</a> and <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-ds/#interactive-models">Nintendo DS</a>, here are two examples of models designed for the PSP. <strong>remote port</strong> at the bottom-left corner (next to the audio jack).</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/bottom.f2a565a2ac74c97efc587423833b9ff3c35f4e648faaa767e90e18c1401e5440.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/bottom.f2a565a2ac74c97efc587423833b9ff3c35f4e648faaa767e90e18c1401e5440_hu_fc9759080184d111.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/bottom.f2a565a2ac74c97efc587423833b9ff3c35f4e648faaa767e90e18c1401e5440_hu_35666e79ed3fa73f.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/bottom.f2a565a2ac74c97efc587423833b9ff3c35f4e648faaa767e90e18c1401e5440_hu_b2d0243ebb5bceb0.webp 1111w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1111" height="560" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/bottom.f2a565a2ac74c97efc587423833b9ff3c35f4e648faaa767e90e18c1401e5440.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Bottom-right corner of the PSP (3000 model) showing the proprietary ‘Video Out’.</figcaption></figure><p>The remote port uses the RS-232 protocol <sup id="bibref:16"><a href="#bib:io-nil" role="doc-biblioref">[16]</a></sup>, an old standard for transferring data in serial. Though the specification wasn’t publicly available to developers (let alone documented), a couple of audio headsets with control buttons appeared on the market. They apparently use the serial port to send commands (play, pause, etc.) to the console.</p></div><p>In later models (2000 and 3000), the remote port was expanded with an extra YCbCr pinout. Sony shipped three <strong>video cables</strong> (component, S-Video and composite) that rely on this interface to enable users to see the contents of the PSP screen on the TV.</p><p>The video cable will send a frame with a resolution of <strong>720x480 pixels (in NTSC) or 720x576 pixels (in PAL)</strong>, in progressive or interlaced mode (the latter option is only available on the 3000 model). As the PSP’s resolution is 480x272 pixels, games will show <strong>black bars</strong> to correct the aspect ratio. However, the bars won’t show when the console is running the ‘XMB’ visual shell, which natively supports adjusting its resolution according to the video cable.</p><hr><h2 id="audio">Audio</h2><p>(Please note that there isn’t space to define and explain every term used in this section. Where a term is uncommon, you can usually find a more comprehensive explanation in other articles from this series. I’ve put links where I can.)</p><p>In this section we tend to encounter a <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/master-system/#audio">PSG</a>, <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#audio">sequencer</a> or a <em>large</em> <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-ds/#audio">mixer</a>. This is because, at the end of the day, dedicated audio hardware is meant to offload audio operations from the CPU. Although if this hardware turns out to be ‘weak’, it degrades the sound capabilities of the console.</p><p>Now, what we consider ‘sound hardware’ in the PSP is very bare-bones: only <strong>two PCM channels and a stereo mixer</strong>. The maximum sampling rate and resolution are <strong>48 kHz</strong> and <strong>16-bit</strong>, respectively.</p><p>I don’t see any of the accelerators I mentioned in the first paragraph. So, does this imply that the sound will be as limited as <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#secrets-and-limitations-1">other</a> <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#audio">cases</a> showed? No! Because the hardware of the PSP enables to compensate it with more software.</p><p>You see, while there isn’t a large amount of sound-related circuitry, Sony supplied a lot of general-purpose components. These can help with audio decoding, streaming and mixing. I’m talking about the <strong>Media Engine</strong>.</p><p>That block is very good at signal processing, but it needs to be programmed. So, Sony wrote the following software for the Media Engine to complement the two PCM channels (we’ll call these the ‘endpoint’) <sup id="bibref:17"><a href="#bib:audio-sad" role="doc-biblioref">[17]</a></sup> <sup id="bibref:18"><a href="#bib:audio-sas" role="doc-biblioref">[18]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li><strong>Sound driver</strong>: talks to the endpoint and performs memory transfers using DMA.</li><li><strong>Software audio synthesizer</strong>: as the name indicates, it generates the signals to be sent to the endpoint.<ul><li>This synthesizer supports 32 channels, using the <strong>PCM</strong>, <strong>ADPCM</strong> or <strong>ATRAC3</strong> formats <sup id="bibref:19"><a href="#bib:io-edepot" role="doc-biblioref">[19]</a></sup>.</li><li>Provides <strong>digital reverb</strong>, <strong>pitch control</strong> and <strong>ADSR envelope</strong>.</li></ul></li></ul><p>Games don’t have access to these modules directly. Instead, they call many libraries included in the official SDK. Some libraries are designed to operate raw signals while others are optimised for particular applications. Examples include:</p><ul><li><strong>MP3 and AAC decoding</strong>.</li><li><strong>MIDI sequencing</strong>.</li><li><strong>VoIP audio decoding</strong> (G729 and u-law).<ul><li>The operating system of the PSP bundled a variant of the ‘Skype’ app, if you wonder what uses VoIP could have here.</li></ul></li></ul><h3 id="audio-comparison">Audio comparison</h3><p>Let’s put all this into practice by taking a look at how games reproduced their sound. I wrote this special player that allows you to swap between consoles (to enable side-by-side comparisons):</p><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft"><table class="audio-switcher" cellspacing="0"><tbody><tr id="_selection" class="audio-selector-group"><td audio="source1">Nintendo DS</td><td audio="source2">PSP</td></tr><tr class="audio-player-group"><td colspan="2"><audio controls="" controlslist="nodownload nofullscreen noplaybackrate noremoteplayback" class="active" loop=""><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/psp/overworld_nds.7839543186a5485ddd91496ea1c48f25991453b39ff76bf3f68e3907639d7166.ogg" type="audio/ogg" preload="metadata"><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/psp/overworld_nds.5a93a3c5be681ae14984cbe070d85a4011c9f21cc46564b4eb653fb665d26268.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" preload="metadata">No support for audio.
</audio><audio controls="" controlslist="nodownload nofullscreen noplaybackrate noremoteplayback" loop=""><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/psp/overworld_psp.d5c68630c05b6fbd8cfdd5146ba311a1d6cf14022b5b19f3a681c4beb3cefde2.ogg" type="audio/ogg" preload="metadata"><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/psp/overworld_psp.56bf37b80833fa01e017f5c6caa38b74d8eaccfc2de779da16439b6c40279c16.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" preload="metadata">No support for audio.</audio></td></tr><tr><td colspan="3" id="_selection_footer" class="audio-footer clickable">Tap to enable interaction</td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="caption"><strong>Nintendo DS:</strong> Final Fantasy IV (2007).<br><strong>PSP:</strong> Final Fantasy IV - The Complete Collection (2011).</figcaption></figure><figure class="toright"><table class="audio-switcher" cellspacing="0"><tbody><tr id="_selection" class="audio-selector-group"><td audio="source1">PlayStation 2</td><td audio="source2">PSP</td></tr><tr class="audio-player-group"><td colspan="2"><audio controls="" controlslist="nodownload nofullscreen noplaybackrate noremoteplayback" class="active" loop=""><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/psp/encounter_ps2.f9ad7e424ff490f173302dc9d1519717f69292518d1117d49fb0c6647819e836.ogg" type="audio/ogg" preload="metadata"><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/psp/encounter_ps2.8c75d003c85f93bcc070b889f8d447aaeabc8e0bb2ad53cd07cf564998606b47.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" preload="metadata">No support for audio.
</audio><audio controls="" controlslist="nodownload nofullscreen noplaybackrate noremoteplayback" loop=""><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/psp/encounter_psp.ad14634a6f4d644067ba25bbe6d480bd13d76d5699b6bf8dd397a84e3cc63a5e.ogg" type="audio/ogg" preload="metadata"><source src="https://www.copetti.org/audio/consoles/psp/encounter_psp.63bd441439c46ff13087f6c57a3fad08dd981581e94d990dedd05036e43fff9a.mp3" type="audio/mpeg" preload="metadata">No support for audio.</audio></td></tr><tr><td colspan="3" id="_selection_footer" class="audio-footer clickable">Tap to enable interaction</td></tr></tbody></table><figcaption class="caption"><strong>PlayStation 2:</strong> Kingdom Hearts 2 (2005).<br><strong>PSP:</strong> Kingdom Hearts Birth by Sleep (2010).</figcaption></figure></div><p>In the first example, the Nintendo DS game sequences its music on the fly, while the PSP one decodes ATRAC3. As you can hear, having no dedicated sound hardware <em>per se</em> doesn’t imply poor sound quality. In fact, one could argue the opposite, as the Media Engine provided more features than the sound chips of most previous portable consoles ever did.</p><p>The second example is much trickier to quantify. I placed a PS2 tune for comparison, but I had to boost the PS2 one a bit (I presume PSP soundtracks are louder to compensate for the smaller speaker and the proximity to the user). Also, bear in mind that the arrangements are slightly different between platforms. It’s possibly just a creative change since the PSP game was released five years after the PS2 one. Overall, the PSP doesn’t show deterioration (considering that the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#audio">PS2’s SPU2</a> is very powerful and flexible).</p><hr><h2 id="io">I/O</h2><p>The PSP has plenty of connections and sensors. However, this section will be a good opportunity to introduce some chipsets that haven’t been mentioned yet. These play a big part in handling the circuitry that detects the player’s input.</p><h3 id="internal-interfaces">Internal interfaces</h3><p>Most of the I/O available is linked in the <strong>Peripheral Bus</strong>. It’s only 32 bits wide, which is enough to transfer simple information at a normal pace. It has access to the main RAM as well.</p><p>The D-pad, joystick and buttons are handled by a unique chip referred to as <strong>‘System Control’ or SysCon</strong>. This is a common codename in Sony’s hardware and it deals with interfacing many internal components – in this case, only the physical buttons.</p><h3 id="external-interfaces">External interfaces</h3><p>The console features a good amount of connections <sup id="bibref:20"><a href="#bib:io-edepot" role="doc-biblioref">[20]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li><strong>802.11b WiFi</strong>: either connects to a hub or operates in ‘ad hoc’ mode to talk to nearby PSPs. This is similar to what the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-ds/#freedom-of-interaction">Nintendo DS</a> offered.</li><li><strong>USB 2.0</strong>: for accessories or to plug the console into a computer. In the case of the latter, the PSP is recognised as a mass storage device, providing access to the memory stick.</li><li><strong>IrDA</strong>: stands for ‘Infrared Data Association’, similar to what a TV remote uses to change the channel. Before the release of the PSP, the infrared protocol was popular for transferring multimedia between a camera/phone and the computer. As for the PSP, however, the IrDA port went bluntly ignored.<ul><li>As tends to happen, Sony removed it with the second revision of the PSP (2000).</li></ul></li></ul><h3 id="commercial-accessories">Commercial accessories</h3><p>The use of a standard port, USB, enabled other companies to design accessories for this console.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/top.fffc4aec2d9de21c44f0d8a48ad9fe4d0294a97f364faa56d72632ff85f21e46.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/top.fffc4aec2d9de21c44f0d8a48ad9fe4d0294a97f364faa56d72632ff85f21e46_hu_a3640ab2ccdc48c2.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/top.fffc4aec2d9de21c44f0d8a48ad9fe4d0294a97f364faa56d72632ff85f21e46_hu_970cfc1f9f6f7d2.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/top.fffc4aec2d9de21c44f0d8a48ad9fe4d0294a97f364faa56d72632ff85f21e46_hu_4cfe35d6274d983a.webp 1111w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1111" height="347" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/psp/io/top.fffc4aec2d9de21c44f0d8a48ad9fe4d0294a97f364faa56d72632ff85f21e46.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Top side of the PSP (model 3000).<br>Notice the two holes surrounding the mini USB port to hold an accessory.</figcaption></figure><p>Examples of commercialised accessories include:</p><ul><li>A <strong>microphone</strong> for audio chatting.</li><li>A <strong>GPS antenna</strong>: apart from navigation, I don’t know what else can you do with it.</li><li>A <strong>camera</strong>: a good addition for the microphone to achieve videoconferencing. This makes sense as Skype was even embedded in the system.</li></ul><p>The funny thing is that these gadgets were also available for Pocket PCs and PDAs as well. It makes you wonder if Sony envisioned the PSP as a <em>Pocket PC for youngsters</em>.</p><h3 id="home-console-connectivity">Home console connectivity</h3><p>After the release of the PlayStation 3, a new feature appeared on the PSP: <strong>Remote Play</strong>. Using a WiFi connection, the PS3 could be remotely controlled from the PSP.</p><p>This was many years before the Wii U launched, eh? Unfortunately, only a handful of PS3 games supported Remote Play, meaning users could only navigate through the menus, do some multimedia and play PlayStation 1 games.</p><hr><h2 id="operating-system">Operating System</h2><p>Over the years, the program in charge of controlling a given console before a game starts has become more and more convoluted – mainly due to the increasing need for security and services (updatable APIs, online multiplayer, multimedia, etc.). The PSP will try to fit all of that in very constrained hardware. Now, I don’t mean to say that the result will be <em>mediocre</em>, but many decisions are the result of balancing costs, performance and robustness.</p><h3 id="architecture-and-design">Architecture and design</h3><p>First and foremost, the PSP contains a hidden, undocumented <strong>4 KB ROM</strong> inside Tachyon where the boot-loader is. In other words, upon powering on, the CPU will start by looking for instructions in there. That ROM has many names, including ‘Bootrom’, ‘Pre-IPL’ and ‘Lib-PSP iplloader’. The latter is the internal codename used by Sony.</p><p>The rest of the system is installed on <strong>32 MB of NAND Flash memory</strong> found in the motherboard. Here is where the majority of the PSP’s Operating System (OS) resides.</p><p>The OS is composed of the following components:</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-2-1-modules-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-2-1-modules">Modules</a></li><li id="tab-2-2-kernelipl-link"><a href="#tab-2-2-kernelipl">Kernel/IPL</a></li><li id="tab-2-3-other-parts-link"><a href="#tab-2-3-other-parts">Other Parts</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-2-1-modules"><h4 id="tab-2-1-modules" class="tab-title">Modules</h4><p>A <strong>module</strong> is what we would call a ‘program’ or ‘driver’ in the PC/Windows world. Once loaded, modules may reside in memory and perform the following tasks <sup id="bibref:21"><a href="#bib:cpu-naked" role="doc-biblioref">[21]</a></sup>:
- Expose functions to simplify access to certain hardware.
- Run as a foreground program (i.e. games).</p><p>A module binary may be encrypted or decrypted. It also embeds metadata to define whether it’s a ‘user module’ or ‘kernel module’; the latter allows the new module to control privileged areas in memory (where the kernel resides).</p><p>Modules are summoned by the ‘kernel’ or ‘Visual Shell’ (VSH). User modules can execute other modules at the discretion of the kernel. This enforces security – the kernel will never load kernel modules from Universal Media Disks (UMDs), for instance.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-2-kernelipl">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-2-kernelipl"><h4 id="tab-2-2-kernelipl" class="tab-title">Kernel/IPL</h4><p>While this OS doesn’t contain a kernel <em>per se</em>, it has multiple components that fill in the duties of a traditional kernel.</p><p>The first component is the <strong>IPL</strong>, which is loaded by the Pre-IPL and takes care of initialising the hardware. Part of the IPL, called <strong>IDStorage</strong>, also stores unique information about the console (such as its MAC address, serial number and UMD authentication keys) <sup id="bibref:22"><a href="#bib:operating_system-jas" role="doc-biblioref">[22]</a></sup>. Overwriting this last area causes catastrophic results! So the UMD keys are duplicated a couple of times, to survive corruption.</p><p>The IPL then loads a set of <strong>kernel modules</strong> which handle low-level operations (memory management, multi-threading and file-system). They also implement memory access exceptions triggered by the MPU (remember the <a href="#focused-memory-management">segmentation paragraph</a>?). For the sake of simplicity, whenever I use the word ‘kernel’ in this article, I’ll be referring to these kernel modules.</p><p>Having said that, the kernel doesn’t do multitasking, but it does implement cooperative multi-threading for single processes.</p><p>The kernel will persist in memory as long as the console has power, which is related to the fact that <strong>programs (user modules) aren’t written for bare-metal</strong>. Instead, user modules rely on functions exposed by kernel modules. Consequently, the kernel reserves <strong>4 MB of main RAM</strong> and another <strong>4 MB for ‘volatile memory’</strong> (temporary buffer for many operations, with access granted at request). That only leaves <strong>24 MB of main RAM</strong> (out of 32 MB) for user programs.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-1-modules">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-3-other-parts">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-3-other-parts"><h4 id="tab-2-3-other-parts" class="tab-title">Other Parts</h4><p>NAND also houses other sections of the firmware.</p><p>Firstly, there’s the <strong>Visual Shell</strong> or ‘VSH’, which is the first thing the user notices after powering on the PSP. The VSH is a graphical user interface that allows the user to run games and other modules (only user-type ones). It is composed of multiple modules, some of which are only loaded upon request.</p><p>As a curious fact: the system call used to boot retail games will first reboot the console, and then load the executable. Possibly to unload the VSH and free up resources for the game.</p><p>Secondly, there is a second partition in NAND that stores user-related data, such as network settings. This partition is called ‘flash1’ (as opposed to ‘flash0’) and its content is referred to as <strong>system settings</strong>.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-2-kernelipl">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="boot-process">Boot process</h3><p>Now that we’ve identified the main parts, let’s see how they organise to put the console into a ‘working state’ once we switch it on. Security is only briefly discussed here; the next section goes into more depth.</p><p>The <em>complex</em> boot process works as follows <sup id="bibref:23"><a href="#bib:operating_system-ipl" role="doc-biblioref">[23]</a></sup> <sup id="bibref:24"><a href="#bib:cpu-naked" role="doc-biblioref">[24]</a></sup>:</p><ol style="list-style-type:decimal"><li>The main CPU’s reset vector is at <code>0x1FC00000</code>, which points to the Pre-IPL ROM inside Tachyon.<ol style="list-style-type:decimal"><li>The first half of the Pre-IPL tells the CPU to copy the other half to scratchpad memory and continue execution from there.<ul><li>The Pre-IPL will now look for the next stage from either <strong>NAND or an external memory stick</strong>. When the latter is selected (never under normal use), the PSP enters a mode called <strong>factory service mode</strong>. For simplicity, we’ll focus on the normal mode (selecting NAND).</li></ul></li><li>The Pre-IPL initialises the NAND controller and continues execution from NAND. The second part of the Pre-IPL runs the IPL, which is encrypted, so it will be decrypted (using ‘KIRK’, more details later) and copied to eDRAM (in the Graphics Engine) as a working area.</li><li>Once finished decrypting, it continues execution at eDRAM, where the decrypted IPL is.</li></ol></li><li>The IPL’s execution process is divided into three stages.<ol style="list-style-type:decimal"><li>The first stage, called the <strong>loader</strong>, resets the main CPU and hides the Pre-IPL ROM from the memory map. The loader also initialises minimal hardware and decompresses ‘Main.bin’, the next stage, on eDRAM.</li><li><strong>Main.bin</strong> focuses on initialising the rest of the hardware, including main memory. Once it finishes, it decrypts the third stage onto main memory and continues execution from there.</li><li>The final stage, referred to as <strong>payload</strong>, loads the kernel. The kernel is stored in the form of different binaries, modules and meta-data that, once loaded into main RAM, will give life to the system. Afterwards, the interactive shell is shown.</li></ol></li></ol><h3 id="visual-shell">Visual Shell</h3><p>This console debuts (at least, internationally speaking) the famous <strong>XrossMediaBar</strong> or ‘XMB’. This is the feature-rich GUI that was shipped with the PSP.</p><div class="tabs nested centered-container"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-2-1-home-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-2-1-home">Home</a></li><li id="nestedtab-2-2-multimedia-link"><a href="#nestedtab-2-2-multimedia">Multimedia</a></li><li id="nestedtab-2-3-game-link"><a href="#nestedtab-2-3-game">Game</a></li><li id="nestedtab-2-4-settings-link"><a href="#nestedtab-2-4-settings">Settings</a></li><li id="nestedtab-2-5-keyboard-link"><a href="#nestedtab-2-5-keyboard">Keyboard</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-2-1-home"><a allows to run a game, manage saves or search for other PSPs (Game Sharing).<br>When the user steps on the actual game item, the XMB styles itself with assets provided by the game, until the user
